title: Vessantara, read whole
hookLine: the generous prince's tale, read from the white elephant to the homecoming (Jataka 547)

cards: The elephant is white, and the people of the Sivi kingdom say it brings the rain. Envoys arrive from Kalinga, a land dried out by drought, and ask the crown prince for it.
He pours water over their hands to seal the gift and hands the elephant over. By evening the city is furious, and the king is pressed to send his own son into exile. The prince is Vessantara.
Tradition places his tale at the end of the Jataka and tells it as the bodhisatta's last life before the one in which he became the Buddha.

teach.b: Vessantara leaves with his wife Maddi and their two small children, Jali and Kanhajina. He gives away his wealth before he goes, and on the road the chariot and horses too, so the family walks.
They settle in huts on a mountain called Vankagiri.

Then the hardest gift. An old brahmin named Jujaka, pushed by a young wife who wants servants, finds the hermitage while Maddi is out gathering fruit, and asks for the children. Vessantara gives them.
What Maddi finds when she comes home belongs to tomorrow. Then the last test.
The god Sakka arrives disguised as a brahmin and asks for Maddi herself. Vessantara gives her too, and Sakka at once gives her back and shows who he is.
Jujaka leads the children to their grandfather, the king, who ransoms them.

The whole court goes up the mountain, the family is together again, and Vessantara returns as king. In the telling, the earth shakes at his gifts. This is a hard tale, and Buddhists have said so themselves.
In the Questions of King Milinda, a king asks the monk Nagasena: was giving away the children not cruel? Nagasena calls it a gift almost too great to do, made for the sake of awakening.
Some readers hear in it dana, generosity, carried to its edge. Others point out that the tale never hides the cost: the children's fear and the mother's grief are told in full.

teach.h: THE GIFT AND WHAT IT COSTS.
teach.b: Read whole, it holds the gift and what the gift costs, and it ends with everyone home.

how: In Theravada lands the Vessantara tale is retold, chanted and painted, and some communities recite it in full at a yearly festival as a teaching on generosity.

o: the prince who gave away all he was asked for
the brahmin who asked for the children
a king who won his kingdom back in war

games.q: vessantara, read whole: tap the pairs.
p: the old brahmin who asks for the children
asks for Maddi, then gives her back

s: the tale ends with Vessantara still in exile
the family is reunited on the mountain and Vessantara returns as king.
Buddhist texts themselves ask whether the gift of the children was cruel
in the Questions of King Milinda, a king puts that question to the monk Nagasena.
Vessantara gave away only his possessions
he gave the elephant, his wealth and chariot, his children, and even Maddi, whom Sakka gave right back.

games.q: you're the crown prince. envoys from a land in drought ask for the white elephant your people believe brings the rain. what do you do?
o: refuse. the kingdom needs its rain too.
games.why: he gives it, sealing the gift with water poured over their hands. his own city is so angry that he is sent into exile.

practice: Pick one moment from today's tale, the white elephant handed over, the family walking without a chariot, the god giving Maddi back, the reunion on the mountain, and tell it to yourself slowly, in your own words, as if to a child at bedtime.
Notice which scene you chose, and which ones you passed over.

wordCard.voice: Vessantara. The prince who gave away everything he was asked for, told as the bodhisatta's last life before the Buddha. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: dakkhinodaka, the water poured over the hands to seal a gift, as Vessantara does with the white elephant.

carryVoice: Your line: the last life. The gift and its cost, told side by side. Day eight hundred forty-seven, done.
